newsitem.title: FINLAND: Analysts still cautious on newsprint outlook.
newsitem.headline: Analysts still cautious on newsprint outlook.

text.p: A tentatively positive outlook for paper markets from Europe's largest forestry group UPM-Kymmene was greeted cautiously on Thursday by forestry analysts looking at prospects for newsprint.
They said slightly upbeat prospects for the grades in North America and Europe could lend some stability to what remains a volatile paper market, but the outlook was not fully clear.
Some believed the European newsprint market looks set to follow a recovery in the U.S., if there are no surprise capacity increases and the dollar remains stable.
"I believe that newsprint prices will probably rise in Europe because they have shown signs of rising in the United States," analyst Paivi Palomaki of Aktia Bank told Reuters.
She later downgraded her recommendation on UPM, a leading player in newsprint markets but for whom newsprint makes up just over one-tenth of total sales, to "neutral" from "buy".
UPM said it expected an upturn in newsprint in North America to begin boosting European prices later this year.

But some analysts saw stability as more likely: "I don't expect newsprint prices to fall from their current level of about 1,000 Deutschemarks per tonne," said Niels Leth, of Den Danske Bank in Stockholm.
"For prices in Europe to rise, the trend would need support from a stable dollar, so that it would not become profitable for Canadian producers to export to Europe," he said.
He said he expected the dollar to remain stable at around 1.7 to the German mark for the time being.

Supporting newsprint prices, no major capacity increases are slated for Europe, except for a 330,000-tonne machine to be built by Norwegian paper maker Norske Skog in France, and due for completion in early 1999, analysts said.
UPM-Kymmene said European newsprint prices were 15 percent lower on average during the first quarter than a year ago, but steadied early in the year.

"The U.S. economy has been growing fast, and the dollar is strong. That means that the flow of newsprint from North America to Europe has evened out," equities analyst Jussi Hyoty of AG Private Bankers said.

"Right now the European newsprint market is in fairly good balance," Hyoty said. "If one more machine were to come along, it would cause more price pressures," he warned. "The market could hardly tolerate any more than that."

Analysts said a rising trend in newsprint prices and demand could lend some stability to a market recently fraught with volatility and confusion, especially with some other paper grades still under pressure.
"Demand for newsprint doesn't fluctuate as steeply as demand for other grades, because the delivery contracts are long-term," said analyst Gustav Lucander of Aros Securities.

Fine paper is sold in shorter-term deals and prices also tend to be vulnerable to swings in chemical pulp prices: prices for fine grades in Europe were clearly coming under pressure due to capacity increases, analysts said.
UPM-Kymmene on Thursday warned of overcapacity in European fine paper markets in the second half of the year.
